title: Time Line Jumper
context: Grade 5, the pages on how long an activity lasts, when it ends and when it began. An adult sees subtraction and addition of times. What the pages are doing is making a time of day a length of time after midnight, so that starts, ends and lengths can be taken apart, and making a journey that passes 12 midnight go on into the next day.

writeup.why: Find how long an activity lasts by taking clock times after midnight, find an end time and a start by jumping along a time line, and carry a journey past 12 midnight into the next day.
writeup.look: One time line with a mark for every hour, 12 noon and 12 midnight marked on their own, and violet jumps that are dragged along it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Line Jumper' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of jumps made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The time line runs across the middle of the area along y 420 from x 90 to x 1130, with a mark for every hour in near-black ink. The 12 noon mark and the 12 midnight mark are drawn taller as marks of their own, and after a 12 midnight mark the words the next day are written above the line in ink. The times the question gives are set on the line in deep blue, labelled Start where a journey begins and Given otherwise, with the 12-hour time above each mark along y 350 and the hours and minutes after midnight below it along y 500. A jump is violet, labelled Jump, with its length written on it, and it is dragged along the line, the whole hours first and then the minutes. The mark a jump reaches is green, labelled End, and the length found is green, labelled How long, at x 120, y 650. On the third phase the slow clock stands at x 900, y 230, showing a time behind the true one. The jump being placed is amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for h, min, a.m. and p.m. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last line stays as the child left it, with its jumps drawn, its start and end marked and the length beside them in green.

phases.win: the length between the two marks turns green
phases.does: reads each time as hours and minutes after midnight, takes the earlier from the later, and finds the length on the line
phases.goal: how long is the later time minus the earlier time, both written as the hours and minutes after midnight
phases.says: How long after midnight is each time? Now take one from the other.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many hours after midnight is 12 noon?
phases.feels: the two marks joined by a length that lights up on the line
phases.hands: Write two clock times on paper strips. Under each, write the hours and minutes after midnight, and take the earlier from the later. Lay the two strips on a paper time line to check the length.
phases.tries: First rung: set two times in the same hour and find how long. Second rung: set two times in different hours. Third rung: the same task across noon, before the question's own times return.

wrong.why: the hour number of an afternoon time is small, and a small number feels early
wrong.move: takes the earlier time from the later as they stand on the 12-hour clock, so the afternoon time looks smaller
wrong.screen: the answer stays in the slot, both times are drawn again with their hours and minutes after midnight beneath them, and the smaller of the two lengths after midnight lights amber

wrong.why: the columns are worked separately, and the smaller number of minutes looks as if it can be taken from the larger
wrong.move: takes the minutes from the minutes without regrouping when the minutes on top are too few
wrong.screen: the answer stays, the length between the two marks is shown on the line, and the minutes column is lit amber with 1 h broken into 60 min

phases.screen: the time line with a start and an end set on it in deep blue, and the hours and minutes after midnight beneath each
phases.soWhat: a clock time is the hours and minutes after midnight, so how long is the later time taken from the earlier one

phases.win: the mark reached turns green, labelled End
phases.does: drags a violet jump of whole hours, then a jump of minutes, and reads the mark reached
phases.goal: an end time is found by jumping from the start, whole hours first and then the minutes
phases.says: Jump the whole hours first. Then how many minutes are left to jump?
phases.check: Away from the screen: from any start time, which jump do you make first, the hours or the minutes?
phases.feels: the jumps landing one after another on the line, the hours first and then the minutes
phases.hands: Draw a time line on a paper strip with a mark for every hour, and put a start on it. Cut two paper jumps, one of whole hours and one of minutes, and lay them end to end from the start to find the end.
phases.tries: First rung: jump whole hours only. Second rung: jump whole hours and then a few minutes. Third rung: the same task with minutes that pass the next hour mark, before the question's own start returns.

wrong.why: the minutes are added like any numbers, and sixty does not stand out
wrong.move: adds the minutes to the start and stops, even when they pass the next hour
wrong.screen: the child's time stays, the jump of minutes is lit amber where it passes the next hour mark, and the hour is moved on in steps

wrong.why: the jump has a number written on it, and the number looks like a time
wrong.move: types the length of the jump as the end time
wrong.screen: the jump stays, the mark it reaches is lit amber and read out as a clock time in green, labelled End, beside the child's answer

phases.screen: the time line with a start set on it and a length of time to jump
phases.soWhat: an end time is found by jumping from the start, the whole hours first and then the minutes

phases.win: the start turns green, and the forward jump lands on the end
phases.does: drags the jumps back along the line, then checks by jumping forward again, and sets the slow clock behind the true time
phases.goal: a start is found by jumping back from the end; a slow clock shows a time behind the true time
phases.says: Which way do you jump to find a start? Check by jumping forward.
phases.check: Away from the screen: if a clock is slow, does it show a time before or after the true time?
phases.feels: the jump back and the jump forward meeting at the same mark
phases.hands: Put an end time on the paper time line and jump back to a start with the same two paper jumps, then jump forward again to see whether you land on the end. Hold a real clock a few minutes slow and find the true time.
phases.tries: First rung: jump back whole hours from an end. Second rung: jump back hours and then minutes, and check by jumping forward. Third rung: the same task with a slow clock, before the question's own end returns.

wrong.why: most jumps go forward, so forward comes first
wrong.move: jumps forward from the end to find a start
wrong.screen: the child's start stays, it is drawn later than its own end on the line, and the end it was worked from is lit amber beside it

wrong.why: a clock face is trusted as the time
wrong.move: takes the time on a slow clock for the true time
wrong.screen: the slow clock is set beside the true time, the gap between them is drawn as a jump in violet, labelled Jump, and the child's answer stays

phases.screen: the time line with an end set on it, a length of time to jump back, and a slow clock beside the line
phases.soWhat: a start is found by jumping back from the end and is checked by jumping forward again, and a slow clock shows a time behind the true time

phases.win: the two jumps are added, the words the next day light up, and the length turns green
phases.does: drags a jump to the 12 midnight mark, drags a second jump on from it, and adds the two lengths
phases.goal: a journey that passes 12 midnight is jumped to 12 midnight first, then on, and is written with the next day
phases.says: Stop at midnight first. What day is it after that?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a journey ends after 12 midnight. Does it end on the day it began, or the next?
phases.feels: the line folding at 12 midnight and the two jumps joining into one length
phases.hands: Fold a paper time line so that it has two days, one on each side of a 12 midnight mark. Jump to the mark, jump on from it, and write the next day on the second part.
phases.tries: First rung: jump to 12 midnight only. Second rung: jump on from 12 midnight to an end. Third rung: the same task with a start in the 12 o'clock hour after noon, before the question's own start returns.

wrong.why: the two times are on the same clock face, so they look like two times of one day
wrong.move: takes a night time from a morning time as they stand, without going through 12 midnight
wrong.screen: the two marks are drawn on two days of the line, the 12 midnight mark between them is lit amber, and the words the next day are written in ink beside the second day

wrong.why: the length is the answer that was asked for, so the day feels like a detail
wrong.move: adds the two jumps but leaves out the words the next day
wrong.screen: the words the next day are lit amber over the line after 12 midnight, and the end time is drawn there

phases.screen: the time line with the 12 midnight mark drawn on its own and the words the next day waiting after it
phases.soWhat: a journey that passes 12 midnight is jumped to 12 midnight first, then on, and is written with the next day

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, as the second jump crosses 12 midnight, the words the next day rise over the far side of the line and the two jumps slide together into one length.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet jumped. On the first phase the time line runs across the area with two clock times set on it in deep blue, each with the hours and minutes after midnight beneath it. On the second a start is set on the line with a length of time waiting to be jumped. On the third an end is set on the line with a length of time to jump back, and a slow clock stands beside the line. On the fourth the 12 midnight mark is drawn on its own with the words the next day waiting after it. One thing moves, once: the first mark, the first jump or the slow clock gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any two times set on the line and jumped between in either direction, past noon and past 12 midnight. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on how long, an end time, a start, a slow clock and a journey past midnight.
voiceLines: A time line with a peg for every hour.
How long after midnight is each time? Now take one from the other.
Jump the whole hours first. Then how many minutes are left to jump?
Which way do you jump to find a start? Check by jumping forward.
Stop at midnight first. What day is it after that?
A new journey on the line. Jump it the same way.
Free play. Set any two times and jump between them.
Look along the line again. Which jump have you not made yet?
You found how long, an end and a start, and you crossed midnight.

observations.why: a time of day is a length of time after midnight.
observations.soWhat: how long is the later time taken from the earlier one, both after midnight.
observations.observe: Each clock time sat on the line with its hours and minutes after midnight beneath it.

observations.why: whole hours land on a mark of the line, so the minutes left are easy to see.
observations.soWhat: jump the whole hours first, then the minutes.
observations.observe: The jump of whole hours was dragged before the jump of minutes.

observations.why: going back and going forward are the same length in opposite directions.
observations.soWhat: check an end or a start by jumping the other way.
observations.observe: A start found by jumping back could be checked by jumping forward again.

observations.why: 12 midnight ends one day and begins the next.
observations.soWhat: a journey that passes 12 midnight is jumped to 12 midnight first, then on, and is written with the next day.
observations.observe: The jump stopped at 12 midnight, and the words the next day lit up after it.

description: Find how long, an end time or a start on a time line by taking clock times after midnight and by jumping, across noon and 12 midnight, and see why a slow clock shows an earlier time.

mods.learn: Learn, adult alongside. Four worked items, one per phase, from how long through the 24-hour clock to a journey past midnight.

source_tool.name: Time Line Jumper
source_tool.blurb: Find how long, an end time or a start on a time line by taking clock times after midnight and by jumping, across noon and 12 midnight, and see why a slow clock shows an earlier time.

serves.exercise: writing the exact time some hours before or after a given time in the recap
finding the time now from an hourly timetable and a departure some minutes ago
filling the missing start time, length of time or end time in a table
finding when a train that left late set off
finding when a guest who came half an hour early arrived
totalling the time of three study sessions one after another

source_tool.description: A time line runs across the working area with a mark for every hour. The 12 noon mark and the 12 midnight mark are drawn as marks of their own, and after a 12 midnight mark the words the next day are written over the line. The clock times the question gives are set on the line in deep blue, labelled Start where a journey begins, with the 12-hour time above the mark and the hours and minutes after midnight below it. On the first phase the two times are set and the length between them is found by taking the earlier from the later, both after midnight, and read in green, labelled How long. On the second phase a violet jump, labelled Jump, is dragged along the line, whole hours first and then the minutes, its length written on it, and the mark it reaches is green, labelled End. On the third phase the jumps go back from an end to a start, and a slow clock beside the line shows a time behind the true one. On the fourth phase the first jump stops at the 12 midnight mark and the jump that goes on is drawn under the words the next day. The jump being placed is amber. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the jumps made.
source_tool.art_direction: A washing line hung with hour pegs / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 5 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look along the line again. Which jump have you not made yet?
voice.onNext: A new journey on the line. Jump it the same way.
voice.opening: A time line with a peg for every hour.
voice.onFinish: You found how long, an end and a start, and you crossed midnight.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any two times and jump between them.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has drawn a time line of the school day on a paper strip and jumped along it with a finger. The tool is what jumps whole hours and then minutes across noon and 12 midnight, and says the next day, which a strip cut at the edge of the day cannot.

answer_key.rule: A clock time is the hours and minutes after midnight, so 1:35 p.m. is 13 h 35 min after midnight. How long is the later time taken from the earlier time, both after midnight. An end time is found by jumping, whole hours first and then the minutes: 1 h 55 min after 11:10 a.m. is 1:05 p.m. A start is found by jumping back the same way. A journey that passes 12 midnight stops at 12 midnight first, then goes on, and is written with the next day: from 10:20 p.m. to 4:35 a.m. the next day is 6 h 15 min. A clock that runs slow shows a time behind the true time, so jump back from the true time by the minutes it is behind.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's jumps where they were dropped. A jump that passes 12 midnight with no stop there shows the 12 midnight mark lit amber and the words the next day missing. A start found by jumping forward stays on the line, and the end it was worked from is lit amber beside it. Two times subtracted as they stand on the 12-hour clock show the afternoon time smaller than the morning one, and the hours after midnight beneath them are lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write each time as the hours and minutes after midnight.
8:20 a.m. is 8 h 20 min after midnight, and 1:35 p.m. is 13 h 35 min after midnight.
13 h 35 min - 8 h 20 min is 5 h 15 min.
So from 8:20 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. is 5 h 15 min.
items.question: How long is it from 8:20 a.m. to 1:35 p.m.?
items.checkpoint: A clock time is the hours and minutes after midnight, so how long is the later time minus the earlier one.
items.misconception: Taking the times apart as they stand on the 12-hour clock, so the afternoon time looks smaller than the morning one.

steps: Jump 1 h from 11:10 a.m. to 12:10 p.m.
Then jump 55 min from 12:10 p.m. to 1:05 p.m.
So 1 h 55 min after 11:10 a.m. is 1:05 p.m.
Check it: 1 h 55 min before 1:05 p.m. is 11:10 a.m.
items.question: A puppet show starts at 11:10 a.m. and lasts 1 h 55 min. When does it end?
items.checkpoint: To find an end time, jump the whole hours first, then the minutes.
items.misconception: Adding the minutes and not moving on to the next hour when they pass 60.

steps: Jump back 2 h from 9:50 p.m. to 7:50 p.m.
Then jump back 25 min from 7:50 p.m. to 7:25 p.m.
So 2 h 25 min before 9:50 p.m. is 7:25 p.m.
Check it: 2 h 25 min after 7:25 p.m. is 9:50 p.m.
items.question: A concert ends at 9:50 p.m. after 2 h 25 min. When did it start?
items.checkpoint: To find a start, jump back from the end, then check by jumping forward again.
items.misconception: Jumping forward instead of back, so the start comes out later than the end.

steps: Jump to 12 midnight first. From 10:20 p.m. to 12 midnight is 1 h 40 min.
Then from 12 midnight to 4:35 a.m. is 4 h 35 min.
1 h 40 min + 4 h 35 min is 6 h 15 min.
So from 10:20 p.m. to 4:35 a.m. the next day is 6 h 15 min.
items.question: A night ferry leaves at 10:20 p.m. and arrives at 4:35 a.m. How long is the journey?
items.checkpoint: When a journey passes 12 midnight, jump to 12 midnight first, then on, and say the next day.
items.misconception: Taking the night time from the morning time as they stand, without going through 12 midnight into the next day.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How long is it from 9:10 a.m. to 11:40 a.m.?
What time is 2 h after 1:20 p.m.?
items.final_answer: 3:20 p.m., because 2 h after 1:20 p.m. is 3:20 p.m.

items.question: A film ends at 8:25 p.m. after 1 h 30 min. When did it start?
items.final_answer: 6:55 p.m., because 1 h 30 min before 8:25 p.m. is 6:55 p.m.

items.question: What time is 30 min after 11:50 p.m.? Say the day.
items.final_answer: 12:20 a.m. the next day, because 30 min after 11:50 p.m. is 12:20 a.m. the next day

items.question: How long is it from 10:25 a.m. to 3:05 p.m.?
A show starts at 4:50 p.m. and lasts 2 h 35 min. When does it end?
items.final_answer: 7:25 p.m., because 2 h 35 min after 4:50 p.m. is 7:25 p.m.

items.question: A clock runs slow by 3 min every hour. It is set right at 7:00 a.m. What does it show when the true time is 11:00 a.m.?
items.final_answer: 10:48 a.m., because in 4 h it runs slow by 4 x 3 = 12 min, and 12 min before 11:00 a.m. is 10:48 a.m.

items.question: A night flight leaves at 11:20 p.m. and lasts 3 h 55 min. When does it land? Say the day.
items.final_answer: 3:15 a.m. the next day, because 3 h 55 min after 11:20 p.m. is 3:15 a.m. the next day

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: is placed on the line at a start, an end or a time given
is dragged along the line by whole hours, then by minutes, forwards or back
shows a time as hours and minutes after midnight
is set behind the true time on the third phase
types a time, a length of time or a day

teaching_notes: Draw a time line for every start, end and length of time, with 12 noon and 12 midnight as marks of their own. Write both clock times as the hours and minutes after midnight, and say so: 1:35 p.m. is 13 h 35 min after midnight. Jump the whole hours first, then the minutes, and check an end time by jumping back to the start. When a jump passes 12 midnight, stop at 12 midnight, carry on, and say the next day. A clock that runs slow shows a time behind the true time: find how far behind, then jump back. Three sessions one after another are totalled by adding their lengths, or by finding how long from the first start to the last end.
generation_prompt: Build a time line tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A time line runs across the stage with a mark for every hour, the 12 noon and 12 midnight marks drawn as marks of their own and the words the next day written over the line after 12 midnight. Clock times given by the question are set on the line in deep blue, labelled Start, with the hours and minutes after midnight beneath them. Violet jumps, labelled Jump, are dragged along the line, whole hours first and then minutes, with their length written on each, and the mark reached is green, labelled End. A length found by taking two times apart is green, labelled How long. A slow clock beside the line shows a time behind the true one. The jump being placed is amber. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the times on the line. Jump the whole hours first and then the minutes, and stop at 12 midnight before going on into the next day.
